facts.text: Abebe Bikila was born on August 7, 1932, in Jato, Shewa.
facts.quote: Abebe Bikila was born on August 7, 1932, in the small community of Jato, then part of the Selale District of Shewa.

facts.text: He was the son of Wudinesh Beneberu and her second husband, Demissie.
facts.quote: Abebe was the son of Wudinesh Beneberu and her second husband, Demissie.

facts.text: During the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, his family was forced to move to Gorro.
facts.quote: During the Second Italo-Ethiopian War (1935–1937), his family was forced to move to the remote town of Gorro.

facts.text: As a boy, Abebe played gena, a traditional long-distance hockey game.
facts.quote: As a young boy, Abebe played gena, a traditional long-distance hockey game played with goalposts sometimes kilometres apart.

facts.text: Around 1952, Abebe joined the 5th Infantry Regiment of the Imperial Guard after moving to Addis Ababa.
facts.quote: Around 1952, he joined the 5th Infantry Regiment of the Imperial Guard after moving to Addis Ababa the year before.

facts.text: Abebe served in the Kagnew Battalion during the Korean War.
facts.quote: Abebe served in the Kagnew Battalion during the Korean War.

facts.text: Swedish coach Onni Niskanen noticed Abebe and began training him for the marathon.
facts.quote: Onni Niskanen, a Swedish coach employed by the Ethiopian government to train the Imperial Guard, soon noticed him and began training him for the marathon.

facts.text: In 1956, Abebe finished second in the Ethiopian Armed Forces championship.
facts.quote: In 1956, Abebe finished second to Wami Biratu in the Ethiopian Armed Forces championship.

facts.text: Abebe married Yewebdar Wolde-Giorgis on March 16, 1960.
facts.quote: Abebe was 27 when he married 15-year-old Yewebdar Wolde-Giorgis on March 16, 1960.

facts.text: Abebe was the first Ethiopian Olympic gold medalist, winning the marathon barefoot at the 1960 Rome Olympics.
facts.quote: He was the first Ethiopian Olympic gold medalist, winning his first gold medal at the 1960 Summer Olympics in Rome while running barefoot.

facts.text: Emperor Haile Selassie awarded Abebe the Star of Ethiopia and promoted him to corporal.
facts.quote: The Emperor awarded him the Star of Ethiopia and promoted him to the rank of asiraleqa (corporal).

facts.text: Following an unsuccessful coup attempt in December 1960, Abebe was briefly arrested and questioned.
facts.quote: Although Abebe was not directly involved, he was briefly arrested and questioned.

facts.text: Abebe ran barefoot for the second and final time at the 1961 Athens Classical Marathon.
facts.quote: This was the second and last event in which he competed barefooted.

facts.text: He finished fifth in the 1963 Boston Marathon.
facts.quote: Abebe ran the 1963 Boston Marathon—which was between his Olympic wins in 1960 and 1964—and finished fifth in 2:24:43.

facts.text: Forty days before the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, Abebe underwent an appendectomy.
facts.quote: He was brought to the hospital and diagnosed with acute appendicitis, and had an appendectomy on September 16.

facts.text: At the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, Abebe won his second gold medal, becoming the first athlete to defend an Olympic marathon title.
facts.quote: At the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, he won his second gold medal, making him the first athlete to successfully defend an Olympic marathon title.

facts.text: After his 1964 victory, Emperor Haile Selassie promoted Abebe to lieutenant.
facts.quote: The Emperor promoted him to the commissioned-officer rank of metoaleqa (lieutenant).

facts.text: In April 1965, Abebe and Mamo Wolde ran a ceremonial half-marathon to the Singer Bowl at the New York World's Fair.
facts.quote: On April 21, 1965, as part of the opening ceremonies for the second season of the 1964–1965 New York World's Fair, Abebe and fellow athlete and Imperial Guardsman Mamo Wolde, ran a ceremonial half-marathon from the Arsenal in Central Park (at 64th Street and Fifth Avenue in Manhattan) to the Singer Bowl at the fair.

facts.text: In July 1967, Abebe sustained a hamstring injury from which he never recovered.
facts.quote: He had injured his hamstring, an injury from which he would never recover.

facts.text: Abebe dropped out of the 1968 Olympic marathon after approximately 16 kilometres.
facts.quote: Abebe had to drop out of the race after approximately 16 km (10 mi) and Mamo Wolde won in 2:20:26.4.

facts.text: A car accident on March 22, 1969, left Abebe paralysed from the neck down.
facts.quote: The accident left him a quadriplegic, paralysed from the neck down; he never walked again.

facts.text: While receiving medical treatment in England, Abebe competed in archery and table tennis at the 1970 Stoke Mandeville Games.
facts.quote: While he was receiving medical treatment in England, Abebe competed in archery and table tennis at the 1970 Stoke Mandeville Games in London.

facts.text: At a 1971 competition for disabled people in Norway, Abebe won the cross-country sleigh-riding event.
facts.quote: He competed in both sports at a 1971 competition for disabled people in Norway and won its cross-country sleigh-riding event.

facts.text: Abebe died in Addis Ababa at age 41 on October 25, 1973, from a cerebral hemorrhage.
facts.quote: On October 25, 1973, Abebe died in Addis Ababa at age 41 of a cerebral hemorrhage, a complication related to his accident four years earlier.

facts.text: Abebe received a state funeral, and Emperor Haile Selassie declared a national day of mourning.
facts.quote: He received a state funeral, and Emperor Haile Selassie declared a national day of mourning.

facts.text: Five years after his death, the New York Road Runners inaugurated the annual Abebe Bikila Award.
facts.quote: Five years after his death, the New York Road Runners inaugurated the annual Abebe Bikila Award for contributions by an individual to long-distance running.
